response.query: What Monte Carlo or bootstrap design and calibration method will produce clinician-meaningful confidence intervals for node strengths and propagated explanations?
response.answer: For clinician-meaningful confidence intervals, use the bootstrap method or randomized quasi-Monte Carlo (RQMC) methods. Bootstrap provides percentile-based confidence intervals, while RQMC offers faster variance convergence.

results.title: [PDF] Confidence Intervals for Randomized Quasi-Monte Carlo Estimators
results.content: Distributed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License Confidence Intervals for Randomized Quasi-Monte Carlo Estimators Pierre L’Ecuyer, Marvin K Nakayama, Art B Owen, Bruno Tuﬀin To cite this version: Pierre L’Ecuyer, Marvin K Nakayama, Art B Owen, Bruno Tuﬀin. ABSTRACT Randomized Quasi-Monte Carlo (RQMC) methods provide unbiased estimators whose variance often converges at a faster rate than standard Monte Carlo as a function of the sample size. A natural solution is to replicate the RQMC process independently a small number of times to estimate the variance and use a standard confidence interval based on a normal or Student t distribution. The RQMC estimator b µn,rqmc = 1 n n−1 ∑ i=0 f(U U Ui) (2) is unbiased for µ, and under similar smoothness assumptions on f as for QMC, its variance converges as O(n−2α+ε) for any ε > 0, where α depends on the smooth-ness of f and on the randomization method [5, 31]. In Section 3, we discuss several ways of computing confidence intervals RQMC estimators, including via a Student t approximation and by applying the bootstrap t. For all these RQMC methods, a standard CLT with a normal limiting distribu-tion holds when n is fixed, b µn,rqmc has finite positive variance, and R →∞, because the RQMC estimator is an average of R iid unbiased estimators. When using R replicates of an RQMC method with n points, at cost nR that is constrained to not exceed a given computation budget, we ex-pect the greatest accuracy in our estimate for large n and small R, while confidence intervals will become more reliable with larger R. In the second step, we generated small samples of R replicates (without replace-ment) from the pool of N values and used them to form all three kinds of confidence intervals from Section 3. The whole process of forming 1000 confidence intervals of each type was done separately for all the integrands, methods, dimensions d, and RQMC sample sizes n = 2k described above. Each confidence interval method was tested in 2400 tasks: 6 integrands, 5 RQMC methods, 4 dimensions, 5 RQMC sample sizes n, and 4 values of the repli-cation size R.

results.title: Monte Carlo Confidence Interval Strategies
results.content: Monte Carlo methods use repeated random sampling to simulate and analyze complex systems and probability models. At its core, Monte Carlo simulation relies on generating a large number of random samples to approximate a desired statistical measure. The reliability of Monte Carlo confidence intervals heavily depends on the sampling strategy. A good Monte Carlo simulation starts with high-quality random number generation. Constructing confidence intervals using Monte Carlo simulations demands careful selection of the estimation technique. Modern statistical programming languages and platforms have built-in support for Monte Carlo simulations and confidence interval estimations. ### MATLAB Examples  MATLAB’s built-in functions offer another avenue for Monte Carlo simulation: - **randn and rand:** For generating random samples. --- ## Performance Analysis  Understanding the performance of Monte Carlo simulations is key to ensuring both the accuracy and efficiency of confidence interval estimation. Monte Carlo-based confidence interval estimation finds practical applications across various fields.
